title: Linux Server Administration
summary: Run a real Linux server the way professionals do: secure remote access, users and permissions, services, firewalls, websites over HTTPS, databases, backups you can restore, monitoring and troubleshooting. Covers both AlmaLinux (Red Hat family) and Ubuntu. Includes graded assignments, a capstone project and a final exam.
outcomes: Connect to servers securely with SSH keys and harden SSH against attack
Manage users, groups, sudo rights and file permissions on the principle of least privilege
Install, update and run software as systemd services, and read their logs
Configure firewalld and ufw so only the services you intend are reachable
Host websites with Nginx or Apache and secure them with free HTTPS certificates
Create databases and least-privilege database users, and keep them off the internet
Build automated backups and prove them with a restore test
Monitor a server, work with SELinux instead of disabling it, and troubleshoot failures methodically
prerequisites:
You should be comfortable using a computer and typing commands carefully. No previous Linux experience is required, but this is a demanding course: plan about **5 hours a week for 8 weeks**.

You need a Linux server you are allowed to break: a virtual machine on your own computer (free), a small rented VPS, or a lab server from your school. The first lesson explains how to set one up.

lessons.title: Finding your way around the filesystem
Module 1 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: Which command tells you which Linux distribution and version a server is running?
questions.explanation: `/etc/os-release` describes the distribution, for example AlmaLinux 9.4 or Ubuntu 24.04. `uname` reports the kernel, not the distribution.

questions.prompt: You connect to a server you have used many times and SSH warns: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED. What should you do?
options: Delete the line from known_hosts and connect anyway
Stop and check with the server's administrator before connecting
Type yes to accept the new key
questions.explanation: A changed host key means the server was reinstalled or someone may be intercepting the connection. Confirm which it is before you trust the new key.

questions.prompt: Your prompt ends with # instead of $. What does that tell you?
options: You are in your home folder
questions.explanation: By convention `#` marks the root account. Every command you type has full power over the system, so take extra care.

questions.prompt: Which directory holds system and service configuration files?
questions.explanation: `/etc` holds configuration, for example `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`. Changing data such as logs and websites lives under `/var`.

questions.prompt: You are in /var/www/site. Which path refers to /var/www/site/public no matter which directory you run it from?
questions.explanation: An absolute path starts with `/` and means the same thing from anywhere. The others are relative to the current directory.

questions.prompt: How do you see hidden files such as .ssh in a directory listing?
questions.explanation: `-a` (all) includes names starting with a dot. `-h` only makes sizes human-readable.

lessons.title: Module 2 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: Working as root, you type: echo 'Port 22' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config. What happens?
options: The line is added to the end of the file
The file is replaced by that single line
Nothing, because echo cannot write files
SSH reloads with the new port
questions.explanation: A single `>` replaces the whole file. `>>` appends. Make a backup copy before editing important files.

questions.prompt: Which command adds the user tobi to the group developers without removing him from his other groups?
questions.explanation: `-a` means append. Without it, `-G` replaces the list of extra groups and can remove someone's admin rights.

questions.prompt: On AlmaLinux, which group's members can use sudo by default?
questions.explanation: Red Hat-family systems use `wheel`; Ubuntu and Debian use `sudo`.

questions.prompt: A file shows -rw-r----- ada webteam. Who can read it?
questions.explanation: Owner `rw-`, group `r--`, others `---`: ada can read and write, webteam members can read, everyone else gets nothing.

questions.prompt: What does chmod 750 give a directory?
options: Owner full access; group can list and enter; others nothing
Owner and group full access; others read
questions.explanation: 7 = rwx for the owner, 5 = r-x for the group (list and enter), 0 = nothing for others.

questions.prompt: To read /srv/site/index.html, what does a user need on the directory /srv/site?
options: Nothing; only the file's permission matters
questions.explanation: A user must be able to enter every directory on the path (`x`) and read the file itself (`r`).

questions.prompt: Several users share /srv/project. What makes new files inside it belong to the project group automatically?
options: The setgid bit on the folder (e.g. chmod 2770)
questions.explanation: The setgid bit on a directory makes new files inherit its group. `777` would let every user on the server write there.

lessons.title: Services with systemd, and the journal
Module 3 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: On Ubuntu, which command actually installs the available updates?
questions.explanation: `apt update` only refreshes the list of available packages. `apt upgrade` installs the updates.

questions.prompt: The load average on a 2-core server stays around 6 for an hour. What does that suggest?
options: Work is queuing: there is more to do than the CPUs can handle
6 GB of memory is in use
questions.explanation: Load counts processes running or waiting. Steadily above the number of cores means processes are waiting for CPU (or for disk).

questions.prompt: Which signal asks a process to finish its work and exit cleanly?
questions.explanation: `TERM` is the polite request and the default for `kill`. `KILL` gives the process no chance to clean up and should be a last resort.

questions.prompt: You started nginx with systemctl start nginx. After a reboot it is not running. Why?
options: It was started but never enabled
questions.explanation: `start` runs it now; `enable` makes it start at boot. Use `systemctl enable --now` to do both.

questions.prompt: How do you see the last 50 log messages from the nginx service?
questions.explanation: `journalctl -u <unit>` filters the journal to one service; `-n 50` shows the last 50 lines and `-f` follows new ones.

questions.prompt: You changed a unit file in /etc/systemd/system/. What must you run before restarting the service?
questions.explanation: systemd caches unit files. `daemon-reload` makes it read your changes.

questions.prompt: Free memory looks very low in free -h, but the available column is large. Should you worry?
options: Yes, the server is about to run out of memory
No, Linux uses spare memory as cache and frees it when programs need it
No, because free -h is always wrong
questions.explanation: Look at **available**. Cached memory counts as used but is handed back when needed.

lessons.title: Networking from the server's point of view
Module 4 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: ss -tulpn shows a database listening on 127.0.0.1:3306. Who can connect to it?
options: Only programs on the same server
Only computers in the same building
questions.explanation: `127.0.0.1` is the loopback address: only the server itself. That is what you want for a database used by a local application.

questions.prompt: Which file on the server lists the public keys allowed to log in to an account?
questions.explanation: `authorized_keys` holds trusted public keys. `id_ed25519` is a private key and must never be copied to servers.

questions.prompt: Before reloading SSH after disabling password login, what is the most important precaution?
options: Keep your current session open and test login in a second session
questions.explanation: If the new settings lock you out, the session that is still open is your way back in to fix them.

questions.prompt: With firewalld, you add a rule with --permanent but it has no effect yet. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Permanent rules are saved to disk but applied only when firewalld reloads.

questions.prompt: On Ubuntu, you are about to run ufw enable on a remote server. What must you do first?
questions.explanation: With a default-deny policy, enabling ufw without allowing SSH would cut off your own session.

questions.prompt: Which SSH setting stops anyone logging in with a password?
questions.explanation: `PasswordAuthentication no` (with `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no`) leaves keys as the only way in. `PubkeyAuthentication no` would do the opposite.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the IP address that a domain name resolves to?
questions.explanation: `dig` asks DNS. `ip a` shows the server's own addresses.

lessons.title: Scheduling with cron and systemd timers
Module 5 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule say?
options: Back up 3 times a day, keep 2 days, 1 copy
3 copies, on 2 kinds of storage, 1 of them off-site
questions.explanation: Three copies, two storage types, one somewhere else, so a single disaster cannot destroy all of them.

questions.prompt: What is the right way to back up a MySQL or MariaDB database that is in use?
options: Take a screenshot of the tables
questions.explanation: A dump with `--single-transaction` gives a consistent copy of InnoDB tables while the site keeps running. Copying the data folder live gives a broken copy.

questions.prompt: Why should a backup be restored as a test regularly?
options: It is the only way to know the backup is complete and usable
questions.explanation: Many backups fail silently: a missing folder, an empty dump, a wrong password. Only a restore proves it works, and tells you how long recovery takes.

questions.prompt: In crontab, what does 30 2 * * * mean?
questions.explanation: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week: minute 30, hour 2, every day.

questions.prompt: df -h shows 40% free space, but the server says No space left on device. What should you check next?
questions.explanation: Millions of small files can use up every inode while bytes remain. `df -i` shows it.

questions.prompt: Why should /etc/fstab use UUID= rather than /dev/vdb1 for a data disk?
options: Device names can change between boots; UUIDs do not
questions.explanation: The kernel can name disks in a different order after hardware changes. The filesystem UUID always identifies the same filesystem.

lessons.title: Module 6 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: After editing an Nginx site configuration, what should you run?
options: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
questions.explanation: Test first; reload only if the test passed. A broken configuration then never reaches the running server.

questions.prompt: Nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway for PHP pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: PHP-FPM is not running or the socket path is wrong
questions.explanation: 502 means Nginx could not get an answer from the backend it passes requests to.

questions.prompt: What does Let's Encrypt need before it can issue a certificate for school.example.org?
options: The domain's DNS points to your server and port 80 is reachable
questions.explanation: The usual HTTP challenge proves you control the domain by fetching a file from it over port 80.

questions.prompt: How long are Let's Encrypt certificates valid?
questions.explanation: They last 90 days and are renewed automatically, usually about 30 days before they expire.

questions.prompt: Which command proves automatic renewal will work, without changing anything?
questions.explanation: `--dry-run` performs a full renewal against the test environment and reports problems.

questions.prompt: Which account should a web application use to connect to its database?
options: A user with rights on that application's database only
Any user, as long as it has a password
questions.explanation: Least privilege: if the application is compromised, the attacker reaches only that database.

questions.prompt: Which setting keeps MySQL/MariaDB from accepting connections from the internet?
questions.explanation: `bind-address = 127.0.0.1` makes the server listen on the loopback interface only. Never use `skip-grant-tables` on a running server: it disables passwords.

lessons.title: Keeping a server secure, and SELinux
Module 7 quiz
lessons.intro: Check what you have learned in this module. You need 70% to pass and you can try as many times as you need. After you pass, you will see an explanation for every question.

questions.prompt: A page under /var/www returns 403 on AlmaLinux even though permissions are correct. You moved the files from your home folder. What fixes it?
questions.explanation: Moved files keep their old SELinux label. `restorecon` gives them the label their location should have, with SELinux still enforcing.

questions.prompt: Your web application must connect to a database on another server, and SELinux blocks it. What is the proper fix?
options: Run the web server as root
questions.explanation: Booleans switch on specific permissions. `-P` keeps the change after a reboot.

questions.prompt: Which command explains recent SELinux denials in plain language?
questions.explanation: `ausearch` finds the denials and `audit2why` explains each one, often naming the boolean or label that fixes it.

questions.prompt: What does logrotate do?
options: Renames, compresses and eventually removes old logs so they do not fill the disk
questions.explanation: It rotates logs on a schedule according to rules in `/etc/logrotate.d/`.

questions.prompt: Why is an external uptime monitor needed in addition to a health-check script on the server?
options: If the server is down, its own script cannot tell you
External monitors are required by Linux
questions.explanation: A server that is off, or cut off from the network, cannot report anything. Something outside must notice the silence.

questions.prompt: Users report the website is down. Following the troubleshooting method, what do you ask early on?
options: Which brand of server is it?
questions.explanation: Most failures follow a change: an update, an edit, a deploy, a full disk. Finding it narrows the search fast.

questions.prompt: Why change only one thing at a time while fixing a problem?
options: Linux allows only one change per hour
So you know which change fixed it and do not add new problems
Logs can record only one change
questions.explanation: If several changes are made together, you cannot tell which one mattered, and an unnecessary change may cause the next outage.

questions.prompt: A teammate says: 'The site works for root but not for the web server. Just chmod -R 777 it.' What is the right response?
options: Agree; it is the quickest fix
Work out which user needs which access, and fix ownership, permissions or SELinux labels for exactly that
Run the web server as root
questions.explanation: 777 makes the files writable by every process, including a compromised one. Grant only what the web server's user needs.

questions.prompt: You must give a deploy user the right to restart one service only. Where and how?
options: A rule in /etc/sudoers.d/ edited with visudo, naming that exact command
questions.explanation: A sudoers rule such as `deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp` grants exactly that, and `visudo` checks the syntax before saving.
